newsitem.title: USA: America Online sees new revenue sources in makeover.
newsitem.headline: America Online sees new revenue sources in makeover.

text.p: America Online Inc., bidding to maintain its lead in the fast-changing world of online services, Monday unveiled the first steps of a major makeover and began selling its stock on the prestigious New York Stock Exchange.

AOL Chairman Steve Case said the world's largest online service wants to stay nimble as the online market keeps changing, keeping its current customers and attracting many new ones even as some industry experts continue to predict its demise due to the rise of the Internet.
"The key context is to recognise that AOL is not getting cocky or complacent," Case told reporters in a conference call to discuss the new initiatives.
"(We want to be) as nimble as we can in a rapidly growing market," he said. "We are re-engineering the interactive experience."

Case earlier participated in the debut of his company's stock on the NYSE, ringing the opening bell on the exchange and, following tradition, buying the first 100 shares of stock sold. The stock, which had traded on Nasdaq under the symbol "AMER.O" is now sold as "AOL.N".
The stock rose $2 to $29 in its NYSE debut.

Case's goal is to reach 10 million members by the end of next year, which he said is achievable because nine out of 10 home computer users are sitting on the sidelines, without an online service. AOL has more than 6 million members, including subscribers in Eurpe and Japan.

This summer, AOL began shipping AOL Version 3.0, an improved version of its software, with more content areas, or "channels," better integration with the Internet's World Wide Web and many other features.

He said AOL plans a big marketing push this fall to trumpet its new software with a big television advertising campaign and an initiative to give members more options for getting help and to attract new members.

Some plans include offering 100 percent guarantees for items bought on AOL with credit cards, sending videos to new and current members on ways to use the service, and other ways to improve its relationships with customers.
"The AOL story is the Internet and more," Case said.
He declined to make any projections on how much AOL will spend on its big marketing push, which begins in October with major prime-time TV advertising.
"We will get into more detail on that later," Case said. "It will be significant."
Case said the "new" AOL will get new revenue from three sources: advertising, transactions and the sale of "private" versions of the AOL service to corporate and organisational networks.

Some corporate and organisational users of the "private" AOL, which will compete with software aimed at internal corporate "intranet" networks, include the Harvard Business School, Hewlett-Packard Co. and Century 21 Real Estate.

Case said AOL has already received $27 million worth of advertising revenue on its online service in the past 45 days, and that the bulk of these revenues would be recognised in the company's total revenues this fiscal year.
He declined to make any forecasts for the new sources of income for AOL, except to say they will become "major sources of revenue," in the hundreds of millions of dollars.
"We believe this industry will move along the same path as other consumer media, moving from (making) all (money from) subscription fees to a variety of revenue streams," Case said.
